title: Iraq's New PM Walks Tightrope With Tehran Visit Days After White House Trip
excerpt: Ali al-Zaidi heads to Iran after securing U.S. business deals and praise from Trump, testing whether Baghdad can chart an independent course between two warring powers.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Iraqi PM Ali al-Zaidi visits Tehran after securing U.S. business deals.
  • Al-Zaidi aims to redefine Iraq's ties with both the U.S. and Iran.
  • Iraq's annual trade with Iran exceeds $12 billion, complicating independence.
  • Al-Zaidi's anti-corruption campaign includes high-profile raids and contract reviews.
  • He is also engaging with Saudi Arabia and Turkey to balance regional relations.
Iraq's Diplomatic Balancing Act
›Iraq's annual trade with Iran exceeds $12 billion.
›Al-Zaidi's U.S. visit resulted in numerous agreements.
›He aims to control Iran-aligned armed groups.
›Al-Zaidi is visiting Saudi Arabia and Turkey this week.

From the Oval Office to Tehran

Just days after wrapping up his first official visit to Washington, where President Donald Trump called him "a fantastic champion," Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi touched down in Tehran on Wednesday for another high-stakes diplomatic stop. The back-to-back visits to the capitals of two countries currently at war with each other encapsulate the tightrope Baghdad has walked since the 2003 U.S.-led invasion toppled Saddam Hussein.

Al-Zaidi, who took office in May as Iraq's youngest prime minister, is a multimillionaire business figure who was considered a compromise candidate within the governing Shia bloc. He was reportedly Washington's preferred option over the more polarizing former Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, whom Trump had repeatedly warned Baghdad against appointing.

His Washington trip yielded tangible results: dozens of agreements and partnerships with U.S. companies and the rehabilitation of a dormant Iraqi-Syrian oil pipeline, a move welcomed by the U.S. State Department. Al-Zaidi spoke of shifting Iraq's relationship with the U.S. from a security-based framework to one built on economic collaboration.

"He is much younger, more business-oriented and not inclined to long speeches, but gets to the heart of the matter, expressing his views, goals and strategy succinctly, clearly and forcefully."

— Zalmay Khalilzad, former U.S. Ambassador to Iraq

The Iran Problem

Iraq's relationship with Iran is deep and complex. Bilateral trade exceeds $12 billion annually, making Iraq one of Iran's largest trading partners. Iraq remains heavily reliant on Iranian natural gas and electricity. Millions of Iranian Shia pilgrims cross the border annually to visit holy sites in Najaf and Karbala, underscoring the profound religious and cultural ties between the two nations.

Since 2003, Tehran has cultivated close ties with influential Shia parties and armed groups in Iraq that form the backbone of the country's security apparatus. These same groups have played a significant military role on Iran's side since the U.S.-Israel war on Iran began in February, putting intense pressure on Baghdad from Washington to rein them in.

Al-Zaidi has vowed to bring these groups under state control, tying their disarmament to the planned withdrawal of roughly 2,000 U.S. troops from Iraq by September 30 — a deadline that experts remain skeptical will hold.

An Anti-Corruption Gambit

Domestically, al-Zaidi has moved aggressively on corruption — an endemic problem his predecessors pledged to address but never did. He ordered sweeping predawn raids on high-level officials, producing dramatic images of confiscated gold and cash. He also ordered a review of major contracts signed by the previous government and created a body to oversee high-value deals.

Former U.S. Ambassador to Iraq Zalmay Khalilzad, who met al-Zaidi during his Washington visit, told The National that the anti-corruption drive could create a "best-case scenario" for Iraq ahead of the U.S. withdrawal. If al-Zaidi can successfully disarm militias, reintegrate them into the mainstream security apparatus, and let the Iraqi armed forces take over, "the issue of withdrawal may not create a challenge or vacuum that Iraq cannot fill," Khalilzad said.

A Regional Balancing Act

Beyond Washington and Tehran, al-Zaidi is also visiting Saudi Arabia and Turkey this week — an itinerary that signals his ambition to present Iraq as a bridge between competing regional powers rather than a proxy for any single one.

One sensitive issue in Tehran will be the future of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups based in northern Iraq, outside Baghdad's direct control. Iran views these groups as a security threat and has repeatedly targeted them in air strikes since the war began in February, demanding that Baghdad prevent them from operating on Iraqi territory.

An adviser to al-Zaidi has said Iraq could serve as "a door to the West" for Iran, while reports suggest the prime minister has offered to mediate between Washington and Tehran.

What It Means for the Region

For India's diaspora community, Iraq's diplomatic trajectory carries significance. India has long maintained strong energy ties with both Iraq and Iran, and stability in the Persian Gulf directly affects oil prices, energy security, and the millions of Indian workers employed across the region. Any shift in Iraq's foreign policy orientation — toward greater independence or closer alignment with either power — ripples through trade routes and labor markets that Indian families depend on.

The larger question, as Al Jazeera noted, is whether Iraq's new leadership can gradually assert greater independence while preserving its strategic partnerships with both sides. For now, al-Zaidi appears to be playing the long game — one diplomatic stop at a time.
